ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — History and Physical — Winston Churchill — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

text.paragraph: Primary care transition visit eight days after a minor ischemic stroke [S]
This fictional modern episode addresses the presenting concerns below. [S]

list.item: Wants to return to full work and to give a major speech within about three months. [S]
Fears another stroke, but does not want to give up cigars or his drinking habits entirely. [S]

text.paragraph: Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Winston Churchill was born on 30 November 1874 at Blenheim Palace, Oxfordshire, and died in London on 24 January 1965. He was Prime Minister from 1940 to 1945 and from 1951 to 1955, when poor health forced him to resign. [D]

In December 1941, during a visit to the White House, Churchill developed dull chest pain after opening a window with great effort. His physician interpreted it as a heart attack, but a cardiologist found no evidence of heart disease, and a later review judges the symptoms probably musculoskeletal. [R]
His most critical episode of pneumonia was in December 1943 in Tunis; it was treated with sulfonamides, which proved effective. [D]

Churchill had his first stroke in 1949, a less serious attack in August 1949 while staying at Cap d'Ail that his physician described as spasm of a small artery. He was seen on multiple occasions from 1950 to 1952 for further cerebrovascular episodes, including transient ischemic attacks. [D]

On the evening of 23 June 1953, while hosting a dinner at 10 Downing Street, Churchill had a stroke consisting of a left hemiparesis, with sagging of the left side of the mouth and impaired articulation. The deficit was greatest about three days after onset, then fluctuated and gradually recovered; the course is consistent with a small lacunar infarct. [D]

The 1953 stroke was concealed at the time: no member of the Cabinet noticed anything wrong at the dinner, and nothing about it was published until Churchill mentioned it about a year later. It has not been a secret since his physician's account was published in 1966. [D]
During the convalescence he was described as very despondent, with spells of apathy, and he wept readily when moved, for example by poetry. [D]
His physician diagnosed clinical depression, which became accepted lore as Churchill's "black dog"; the 2020 study by Vale and Scadding argues convincingly against this diagnosis. [R]

Smoking and alcohol were long-standing risk factors. A 1943 fluid chart listed champagne 10 oz, brandy 2 oz, and whisky and soda 8 oz, and accounts of the 1953 convalescence describe his usual cigar and whisky and soda. [D]

His father, Lord Randolph Churchill, died in 1895 aged 45 after a progressive illness with speech and hearing problems, dizziness, palpitations, and numbness of the hands and feet. Syphilis was long assumed; a brain tumor has been argued as more likely, and the cause cannot be determined with certainty. [R]

text.paragraph: 3 later historical claims are omitted because they describe events after the index age. See the teaching note.
Historical biography with true dates. These events are not part of the synthetic care timeline.

Activity: little planned exercise; walks about the house and garden; afternoon nap most days [S]
Supports: married and lives with his spouse; adult children; a large, devoted staff [S]

text.paragraph: Positive for the concerns in the history of present illness. Alert, articulate, and quick-witted; speech mildly slurred in long sentences at intake. Mood low at times since the stroke, with apathy and poor sleep; tears up readily when moved by poetry or music, more than before; denies thoughts of death or self-harm; PHQ-9 8, item 9 scored 0. No other systems reported as affected in this synthetic episode. [S]

text.paragraph: Alert and engaged. Walks with a stick outdoors; left hand clumsy with buttons and writing; independent in self-care with extra time; modified Rankin Scale about 2 at intake. Walking without a stick, writing normally, and back at full work by about three months; modified Rankin Scale 1. [S]

Aspirin with clopidogrel for 21 days after the minor stroke, then clopidogrel 75 mg alone. Guideline: 2021 Guideline for the Prevention of Stroke in Patients With Stroke and Transient Ischemic Attack (2021); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, stroke/TIA, hypertension, and depression monographs (2026) [S]

Atorvastatin 80 mg with a lipid panel 4 to 12 weeks after starting, aiming for LDL cholesterol below 70 mg/dL. Guideline: 2021 Guideline for the Prevention of Stroke in Patients With Stroke and Transient Ischemic Attack (2021); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, stroke/TIA, hypertension, and depression monographs (2026) [S]

Lower blood pressure below 130/80 with amlodipine and lisinopril, checking standing blood pressure at each visit and a basic metabolic panel 1 to 2 weeks after starting lisinopril. Guideline: 2021 Guideline for the Prevention of Stroke in Patients With Stroke and Transient Ischemic Attack (2021); 2025 AHA/ACC/AANP/AAPA/ABC/ACCP/ACPM/AGS/AMA/ASPC/NMA/PCNA/SGIM Guideline for the Prevention, Detection, Evaluation, and Management of High Blood Pressure in Adults (2025); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, stroke/TIA, hypertension, and depression monographs (2026) [S]

Neurology consultation to confirm the stroke mechanism, set the antiplatelet plan after the 21-day course, decide on prolonged cardiac rhythm monitoring, and advise on return to work and public speaking. Guideline: 2021 Guideline for the Prevention of Stroke in Patients With Stroke and Transient Ischemic Attack (2021); 2024 ACC Expert Consensus Decision Pathway on Practical Approaches for Arrhythmia Monitoring After Stroke (2024) [S]

Outpatient physical and occupational therapy for left-sided weakness, with fall-risk review at every visit. Guideline: Primary Care of Adult Patients After Stroke: A Scientific Statement From the American Heart Association/American Stroke Association (2021); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, stroke/TIA, hypertension, and depression monographs (2026) [S]

PHQ-9 at the first visit and at each review while symptoms persist, MoCA again within the first year, and attention to post-stroke tearfulness. Guideline: Primary Care of Adult Patients After Stroke: A Scientific Statement From the American Heart Association/American Stroke Association (2021); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, stroke/TIA, hypertension, and depression monographs (2026) [S]

Brief interventions at every visit for unhealthy alcohol use (AUDIT-C, no more than two drinks a day) and cigar smoking, with nicotine replacement offered. Guideline: 2021 Guideline for the Prevention of Stroke in Patients With Stroke and Transient Ischemic Attack (2021); Tobacco Smoking Cessation in Adults, Including Pregnant Persons: Interventions (2021); Unhealthy Alcohol Use in Adolescents and Adults: Screening and Behavioral Counseling Interventions (2018) [S]

Yearly influenza vaccine and current COVID-19 vaccine. Guideline: 2021 Guideline for the Prevention of Stroke in Patients With Stroke and Transient Ischemic Attack (2021); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, stroke/TIA, hypertension, and depression monographs (2026) [S]
